item.title: Indian police detain 'cockroach' movement founder Dipke ahead of protest
item.description:
Police detained India’s ‘cockroach’ movement founder Abhijeet Dipke on Friday, live images from his group showed, ahead of a protest called by him in capital Delhi’s central business district, the latest rally to demand the resignation of India’s election chief.

The youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), opposition groups, and student organisations have held almost daily protests this month demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation over a revision of voter lists that critics say favours Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

More than 130 million voters were deleted during the revision but the Election Commission has denied favouring any party and said wrongly deleted voters can re-enrol. The BJP has accused rivals of trying to undermine democracy by wrongly questioning legitimate electoral processes.

Dipke called Friday’s protest in support of two CJP leaders detained and sent to jail this week for five days for demonstrating at a protest site in violation of a ban.

The group and left-wing student organisations had urged supporters to gather at the Central Park in New Delhi’s busy Connaught Place shopping and food district on Friday evening to wave and hoist the national flag.

The live video on CJP’s Instagram handle showed Dipke coming out of a house and walking towards the street, where police officers stopped him and, after a brief argument, hauled him into a police car and drove away.

“We are detaining you right now,” a police officer could be heard telling Dipke.

“I have not broken any law right now…how can you detain me?” Dipke asked the police officers as he was taken away.

There was no immediate comment from the police on the detention.

Earlier on Friday, police met Dipke and warned him against going ahead with the protest.

Park closed ahead of protest

Authorities closed the central New Delhi park before the protest over the voter-roll revision, which critics say has disenfranchised millions.

Dipke urged supporters to rally at Central Park after two of his colleagues were detained for breaching security barricades at Jantar Mantar, where they had gone to wave the national flag.

Earlier this week, police removed authorisation for Jantar Mantar as a designated protest site.

On Friday, thousands of security personnel were deployed in parts of the city, with yellow-coloured metal barricades put up at key intersections.

Earlier, Dipke said he was undeterred despite the possibility of being arrested ahead of Friday’s protest.

“Why are you so afraid of cockroaches?” Dipke said.

“I want to tell Narendra Modi that we are not afraid… if waving the Indian national flag lands you in jail, we are ready,” he said Thursday.

Delhi’s municipal authorities said they were closing the Central Park for two days for “administrative” reasons.

Delhi Police have barred public gatherings around Connaught Place citing concerns about public order and safety.

Violation of the orders would “attract suitable legal action”, police said Thursday, but added that they would allow “selected persons” to gather at a “suitable place”.

In recent days, the Indian capital has seen street protests over a large-scale voter roll revision exercise overseen by chief election commissioner Kumar.

Critics say the removals have disproportionately affected minorities, particularly Muslims.

Election authorities say the move was intended to eliminate duplicate, deceased and fraudulent entries.

Members of Modi’s Hindu nationalist BJP have long alleged that large numbers of undocumented Muslim migrants from neighbouring Bangladesh have fraudulently entered India’s electoral rolls.

On Friday, Defence Minister Rajnath Singh dismissed the allegations, saying the sole agenda of the opposition parties was “to destroy democratic institutions and create unrest in the country”.

“Their fight is not for electoral reform… not for Gyanesh Kumar, not for the bright future of the country’s youth,” he said at a news conference.

“Rather, this is their conspiracy to seize power by creating anarchy in the country.”

item.title: The Rohingya case that could redefine the law on genocide
item.description:
The Rohingya case that could redefine the law on genocide

Submitted by Sondos Asem on Fri, 10/16/2026 - 08:00
Judges in the Gambia v Myanmar case are preparing a ruling that will have ramifications for Israel and Gaza

In the first week of September 2017, Antonia Mulvey was on the Bangladesh-Myanmar border, interviewing women and children who had fled across it days earlier.

“Women waited all day to talk to me and they'd had horrific things happen to them,” she told Middle East Eye. “What struck me when I listened to their stories was that they were asking me for justice.”

Mulvey was one of the first three investigators deployed by a UN fact-finding mission. Her brief was sexual violence and crimes against children.

Nine years later, the case that grew out of those accounts is nearing its end, with the International Court of Justice (ICJ) expected to rule in the coming weeks on whether Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya.

Mulvey, now executive director of Legal Action Worldwide (LAW), which represents Rohingya witnesses in the case, said that if the judges rule against Myanmar, it will be the first time the court has found a state responsible for committing genocide.

For many Rohingya, the ruling is about more than the past. “We need to fix the root cause,” one refugee told LAW researchers. “The best justice for us is to fix the root cause of the problem.”

Legal experts say they also expect the outcome to have consequences for other ICJ cases involving allegations of genocide, most pressingly South Africa's case against Israel over its war against Palestinians in Gaza, where the confirmed death toll has reached almost 75,000 people.

Michael Becker, a professor of international law at Trinity College Dublin, described the case as a "crucial opportunity for the ICJ to clarify and develop the law on genocide” which, he said, would have "major repercussions" for the South African case.

Decades of persecution

The Rohingya, a mostly Muslim minority, have lived for generations in western Myanmar’s Rakhine State. Northern Rakhine was the only part of the country where they formed a majority.

Myanmar's 1982 Citizenship Law left the Rohingya off the list of the country's officially recognised ethnic groups, leaving most of them stateless. 

The state and its lawyers refer to the Rohingya as “Bengalis”, a term that casts them as migrants from Bangladesh.

For decades, restrictions on the Rohingya’s movement, marriage rights, education and access to healthcare have been documented. Hundreds of thousands fled to Bangladesh in waves of violence in 1978, and again in 1991 and 1992. 

In 2012, clashes in Rakhine displaced about 140,000 people, most of them Rohingya. Many remain confined to camps around the state capital, Sittwe. 

“Rohingya have been persecuted in Myanmar for decades,” said Salma, a Rohingya survivor who attended the ICJ hearings in January, in comments shared by LAW. She asked that only her first name be used.

For many refugees, justice now means one thing above all: citizenship. In a survey conducted by LAW of just under 500 refugees in the Cox's Bazar camps in Bangladesh, 86 percent of participants said citizenship and the right to identify as Rohingya were necessary for justice. 

“We want [the] international community to destroy the 1982 law, and we hope they will do it,” one participant said. “We had Myanmar citizenship, and we were living there for a long time, and our citizenship should be restored. If they provide these two things, we will get everything.”

“They want justice, but they want citizenship,” Mulvey said. “They want to be acknowledged for what happened, and they want that land and property back.”

'Clearance operations'

On 25 August 2017, Myanmar's military launched what it called “clearance operations” in northern Rakhine State, after the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (Arsa) attacked police posts. 

More than 700,000 Rohingya fled to Bangladesh in the months that followed. About 1.2 million Rohingya refugees now live in the camps of Cox's Bazar.

In 2018, the UN fact-finding mission concluded that there was enough information to infer genocidal intent. It called for senior generals - including then-army chief Min Aung Hlaing, who is now president - to be investigated and prosecuted. 

Mulvey said she drafted the report's sections on sexual violence and crimes against children.

“It was the UN fact-finding mission report that Gambia relied upon in order to initiate proceedings at the ICJ,” she said. 

Abubacarr Tambadou, the Gambia's then justice minister, had spent years as a prosecutor at the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda. He visited the Cox's Bazar camps in 2018. 

In November 2019, backed by the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, the Gambia filed its case.

The West African country had no direct link to the violence. It relied on the principle, accepted by the court in 2022, that every state party to the 1948 Genocide Convention has a common interest in seeing it upheld.

In January 2020, the court unanimously ordered Myanmar to take all measures within its power to prevent genocidal acts. 

A year later, the military seized power. 

In July 2022, the judges rejected Myanmar's objections to the court's jurisdiction, clearing the way for the hearings that took place in January this year.

'It was very silent'

Over three weeks of hearings, the court heard from three Rohingya witnesses in closed session: two men and a woman. They were identified in court only by their initials, and each came from one of three villages at the centre of The Gambia's case: Min Gyi, Maung Nu and Chut Pyin.

Mulvey, their lawyer, said they spoke about the killing of their family members, the sexual violence they had been subjected to and their flight from Rakhine. Two travelled to the Hague from Cox's Bazar and one from Canada, where they had been resettled.

“It was very silent. You could also hear crying. It was extraordinarily powerful testimony,” Mulvey said. “Of course we have to wait to see what the judgment is, but you could feel the weight of it.”

LAW also brought a victims' delegation of three Rohingya survivors to sit in the courtroom: a man, a woman and a hijra, a term used in South Asia for transgender and intersex people. 

Mulvey said it was the first time a transgender survivor had been part of a delegation in the court.

“We did not know that legal proceedings existed, and we could fight for our rights,” Salma, who part of the delegation, said. “But this time, we have the tools to defend ourselves and demand accountability and reparation for what happened to us.” 

Rehana, the delegation's hijra member, who also asked to be identified by her first name only, said she hoped a ruling would include the whole community. “If the genocide is recognised, we hope that we will be getting our justice. Justice for our entire community, including hijra,” she said.

LAW also submitted hundreds of pages of written witness evidence, which Mulvey said The Gambia relied on heavily.

Rape and sexual violence were central to The Gambia's case. “They selected, particularly, women and girls of reproductive age. They gang raped them. That was the method of choice,” Mulvey said, of army soldiers. 

She said investigators found “a pattern of biting, to leave an indelible mark on them”. She said rape in front of the community reflected “the intent to destroy the very social fabric of the community”.

The ICJ has accepted before that rape can be an act of genocide, in Bosnia v Serbia and Croatia v Serbia. But in neither case did it find the intent required to classify those acts as genocide.

A ruling against Myanmar on this point would mark “the first time the ICJ has actually found sexual violence itself to constitute genocide in a merits judgment”, Mulvey said.

What is genocide?

In deciding the case, the judges will draw on the Genocide Convention itself, the court’s own earlier rulings, and the case law of the international criminal tribunals for the former Yugoslavia and Rwanda.

Israel’s war on Gaza: What is the meaning of genocide?
Read More »

The Genocide Convention, adopted by the UN General Assembly in 1948, defines genocide as any of five acts “committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group, as such”. 

In Bosnia v Serbia in 2007, the court held that the intent must be to destroy at least a substantial part of the group, and that it must be physical or biological destruction rather than cultural destruction. 

It also ruled that charges of such exceptional gravity against a state must be proved by evidence that is “fully conclusive”.

Intent can be shown by “particular circumstances” or inferred from a pattern of conduct. But in Croatia v Serbia in 2015, the court set a high bar for inference.

To infer genocidal intent from a pattern of conduct, it said, “it is necessary and sufficient that this is the only inference that could reasonably be drawn from the acts in question”.

Furthermore, applying those tests, the court found in the Bosnia v Serbia case in 2007 that genocide had been committed only at Srebrenica, and that Serbia was responsible for failing to prevent and punish it, not for committing it. 

The Gambia's case

Philippe Sands and Paul Reichler, two lawyers representing the Gambia, argued that Myanmar’s military operations in northern Rakhine State targeted a substantial part of the Rohingya population and that the evidence pointed to an intent to destroy the group.

Sands used Myanmar's own figures from its written pleadings to address whether Myanmar had targeted a “substantial” part of the Rohingya.

'They selected, particularly, women and girls of reproductive age. They gang raped them. That was the method of choice'

- Antonia Mulvey, lawyer

He calculated that 815,459 Rohingya lived in northern Rakhine's three townships, Maungdaw, Buthidaung and Rathedaung, before the 2017 operations. About 700,000 of them, nearly nine in 10, fled to Bangladesh. The military “targeted tens of thousands of homes, and over 800,000 human beings”, Sands said.

Myanmar had argued that the estimated 10,000 to 25,000 people killed did not amount to a substantial part of the group. Sands said those figures were “likely to be an underestimate”. 

Myanmar “has gone out of its way to destroy the evidence, including the evidence of the burial of large numbers of bodies in mass graves”, he said.

“Genocide is not a numbers game,” Sands said, explaining that “there is no magical number of victims which turns one kind of crime into another kind of crime.”

“The 700,000 who fled to Bangladesh for their lives were no less targeted than their murdered brothers and sisters,” the British lawyer said.

Sands also argued that northern Rakhine mattered because it was the one region where Rohingya were the majority. 

Turning to intent, he said that it was proved both by “particular circumstances” and by a pattern of conduct. He pointed first to the three witnesses' villages.

“There is no world in which the shooting of Witness MS's daughter, as she waded across a river to escape, was not genocidal; or the intentional burning of his wife and four other children inside a house,” Sands told the court. 

“There is no world in which the gang rape of Witness NJ, the murder of her infant child in front of her, was not genocidal.”

Myanmar acted with genocidal intent, Sands said, because “its discriminatory policies, its hate speech, its pre-planning and organisation, its extreme brutality, its sexual violence, its targeting of children, its destruction of evidence, its impunity for the perpetrators, its failure to co-operate with the UN, cannot reasonably be understood in any other way”.

The counter-terrorism defence

Reichler addressed what is known as the “only reasonable inference” test, which in this case would require proving whether any explanation other than genocide could reasonably account for what happened in Rakhine.

Myanmar's answer was counter-terrorism. “They have put all their eggs in the counter-terrorism basket,” Reichler said.

He told the court that Myanmar's lead counsel, Christopher Staker, had conceded that genocide can take place during a counter-terrorism operation. 

Even if Myanmar was responding to Arsa, he argued, “the fact that there was a counter-terrorism operation in progress … is pure context. It is not intent.”

The question, Reichler said, was what the state intended “at the time its authorised agents began firing their weapons deliberately at Rohingya civilians, including women and children”.

Reichler then dealt with the other possible explanation: that Myanmar meant to drive the Rohingya out, not destroy them. That was the conclusion the court reached about Serbia and Croatia in 2015.

Reichler cited the testimony of the Gambia’s military expert, who was asked whether the operations could have been ethnic cleansing, rather than genocide. The expert said they could not, because ethnic cleansing does not involve killing a group’s children. 

He added that a force seeking only to drive a population out would not keep shooting at people as they fled, or station troops on the river to sink their boats as they were about to reach Bangladesh.

Soldiers also laid landmines at border crossings after 25 August 2017. The fact finding mission said this showed the mines were “intended to target fleeing Rohingya civilians and to prevent those who had already left from returning”.

Russia, Georgia and forced displacement

Reichler contrasted Rakhine with Georgia v Russia, a case in which he had acted for Georgia. 

In this case, Russian forces ordered ethnic Georgians to leave South Ossetia. Those who complied were not harmed. Fleeing refugees were not shot at and there was no systematic sexual violence. “On those facts, if proven, this was forced displacement, or ethnic cleansing. It was not genocide,” Reichler said.

The wars in the former Yugoslavia were “essentially about the control of territory,” he argued. The Tatmadaw, Myanmar's military, “were not seeking to enlarge Myanmar's territory”.

He warned that Myanmar might “change its narrative in the second round, after we have finished speaking and there is no opportunity for us to respond further”.

Mulvey said that is what happened. Myanmar “did not argue deportation or forcible transfer until the very end of their oral hearings”, she told MEE.

In Myanmar’s final session on 29 January, counsel Stefan Talmon quoted one of The Gambia’s own witnesses, identified as MN, telling the court: “We knew that the military did this to force us out of the country.” From such accounts, Talmon argued, the court could conclude that “the intention of the military was not to destroy them as a people as such but to force them out of the country”.

“There is thus at least one other inference that can reasonably be drawn from the conduct,” he said.

Srebrenica genocide survivors draw parallels with Gaza 30 years after massacre
Read More »

But even if expulsion had been the aim, Reichler argued that the court's own judgments allowed for a genocide finding if the displacement was carried out “with a view to the destruction of the group, as distinct from its removal from the region”.

Reichler argued that other motives, such as fighting Arsa, would not rule out genocidal intent. He noted that in Bosnia the court found genocide at Srebrenica even though the Bosnian Serb leadership's “essential motive” was to create a larger Serb state.

What mattered was the intent at the moment Myanmar soldiers were “segregating and executing men and boys, raping and gang raping women and girls, killing children and infants – tossing them into fires”. 

He said the destruction continued well into 2018, including in more than 180 villages where Myanmar admits there was no Arsa activity, and was followed by bulldozing, resettlement by ethnic Rakhine and the building of military bases.

Mulvey described the same pattern from her own investigations. 

“They would surround the village. Then often in the early hours of the morning when people were asleep, they would fire mortars into the village. They would then proceed by shooting indiscriminately at civilians,” she told MEE.

She said soldiers continued to shoot at people as they fled towards Bangladesh. “What they did was to ensure that they were killed along the way,” she said.

Myanmar rejected all the allegations. It argued that the operations were a lawful response to attacks by Arsa.

What western nations argued

In November 2023, Canada, Denmark, France, Germany, the Netherlands and the UK filed a joint submission to the court in support of the Gambia. 

They were among 11 states that intervened in the case. States that intervene in this way do not comment on the facts, only on how the Genocide Convention should be read.

The six states warned that the “only reasonable inference” test should not be applied so strictly that genocide becomes “near-impossible” to prove, since states rarely put an intent to destroy a group in writing. 

They also argued that the number of people killed should not decide whether genocide took place. Rape, sexual violence and the targeting of children serve no military purpose, so such acts can point strongly to an intent to destroy a group, they wrote. 

The six states added that UN fact-finding reports deserve particular weight as the work of independent investigators.

Both Sands and Reichler cited the submission in their closing arguments.

'Major repercussions for Israel case'

Becker, a professor of international law at Trinity College Dublin, said this was the first time a court would rule on mass human rights violations in a case brought by “a non-injured state acting to uphold international law”.

“Cases like The Gambia v Myanmar have arguably sought to transform the role and function of the ICJ in contemporary affairs. The outcome here may determine whether that trend will continue,” Becker told MEE.

'Whether the ICJ accepts or rejects that view of genocidal intent will have major repercussions for South Africa's case against Israel'

- Michael Becker, law professor

He said the judgment would be “a crucial opportunity for the ICJ to clarify and develop the law on genocide”, particularly on how intent can be established by inference.

“The core of Myanmar's argument is that actions that can reasonably be characterised as a counter-terrorism operation cannot simultaneously be treated as acts of genocide,” he said.

"Whether the ICJ accepts or rejects that view of genocidal intent will have major repercussions for South Africa's case against Israel at the ICJ," Becker explained, "where Israel has similarly claimed that an armed conflict with Hamas precludes a finding that Israel has simultaneously undertaken actions aimed at the physical destruction of the Palestinian population of Gaza.”

Becker said “recent claims that the ICJ may end up 'lowering the standard' to establish genocidal intent are misguided because they fail to acknowledge the ambiguities in the ICJ's pronouncements on genocidal intent”.

He added that the ruling would show how the court treats cases built largely on UN inquiry reports. Myanmar made attacks on the reliability of the fact-finding mission’s reports a central part of its defence, while the Gambia relied on the same reports extensively. 

“If the ICJ shows a reluctance to credit the findings of such reports, this will send a strong signal to South Africa, and potential litigants in other future cases, about the need to find other ways to support their claims,” he said.

A major UN inquiry last year already concluded that Israel was responsible for genocide in Gaza. Its chief investigator, Navi Pillay, told MEE at the time that her report used the same legal standard used by the ICJ in determining a finding of genocide and that it would "bear particular probative value and can be relied upon" by the court.

Israel submitted its response to South Africa's case in March. South Africa's reply is due in November 2027.

What the victims want

Mulvey said she is often asked what a ruling would mean for people in Cox's Bazar “who barely have $1 a day”.

“The short answer is yes, it makes a difference to the community,” she said. “It's important for them that the world's highest court recognises what happened to them.”

Many refugees told LAW researchers that compensation and punishment alone would not be enough. “What is the reason for the issue that happened to us? We need to fix the root cause,” one participant in the survey said. “If we want compensation, their punishment, and such things, I don't think we get our justice.

'For me, justice means truth. It means that perpetrators must be held accountable'

- Samir Sadaf, young Rohingya 

“Justice [meaning citizenship] is important for our children and grandchildren,” one woman who took part in the survey said. “If it prevails, they will have access to education and they will be able to become successful… in Myanmar.”

The Gambia's final submissions reflected some of these demands. It asked the court to order Myanmar to prosecute those responsible and to provide reparations to the victims.

These include safe and dignified return, the restoration of property, the right to identify as Rohingya, and “full and equal citizenship”.

LAW has called for a trust fund for the Rohingya that would be linked to any reparations the court orders.

Samir Sadaf, a young Rohingya man who fled Rakhine as a child, described what justice would mean beyond a court ruling. 

“For me, justice means truth. It means that perpetrators must be held accountable,” he wrote in an article published by LAW. “Where there is justice, there should be safety, equal rights, freedom of movement, and dignity.”

Enforcing the law

ICJ judgments are binding and cannot be appealed, but the court has no means of enforcing them. If a state refuses to comply, the matter can go to the UN Security Council, where China and Russia, both partners of Myanmar's military government, hold vetoes. 

Min Aung Hlaing, who led the 2017 operations, named himself president in April after contested elections.

“While it may prove impossible to enforce such a judgment while Myanmar continues to operate under military rule, compliance with the ICJ judgment may become the price of readmission to the international community,” Becker said.

A ruling that Myanmar breached the convention “can also increase the pressure on third states to disengage from Myanmar until it demonstrates genuine reform”, he said.

Mulvey said LAW's victims' delegation will be in the courtroom when the judgment is read.

Salma, who sat in the court through the January hearings, said the Rohingya would not give up. “We won't go back without justice,” she said.

item.title: India closes down New Delhi park ahead of 'cockroach' movement rally
item.description:
Authorities closed a central New Delhi park Friday before a fresh protest seeking the removal of India’s election chief over a voter-roll revision that critics say has disenfranchised millions.

Organised by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), the campaign has become the focal point of opposition anger over allegations that the revised rolls favour Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling party.

The Election Commission of India, which oversees voting in the world’s most populous nation, has denied any wrongdoing.

CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke urged supporters to rally at the capital’s Central Park after two of his colleagues were detained for breaching security barricades at Jantar Mantar, where they had gone to wave the national flag.

Earlier this week, police removed authorisation for Jantar Mantar as a designated protest site.

On Friday, thousands of security personnel were deployed in parts of the city, with yellow-coloured metal barricades put up at key intersections.

Dipke said he was undeterred despite the possibility of being arrested ahead of Friday’s protest.

“Why are you so afraid of cockroaches?” Dipke said.

“I want to tell Narendra Modi that we are not afraid… if waving the Indian national flag lands you in jail, we are ready,” he said Thursday.

Delhi’s municipal authorities said they were closing the Central Park for two days for “administrative” reasons.

Delhi Police have barred public gatherings around Connaught Place citing concerns about public order and safety.

Violation of the orders would “attract suitable legal action”, police said Thursday, but added that they would allow “selected persons” to gather at a “suitable place”.

In recent days, the Indian capital has seen street protests over a large-scale voter roll revision exercise overseen by chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

More than 130 million names have been removed from electoral lists under the revision exercise, according to media reports.

Critics say the removals have disproportionately affected minorities, particularly Muslims.

Election authorities say the move was intended to eliminate duplicate, deceased and fraudulent entries.

Members of Modi’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party have long alleged that large numbers of undocumented Muslim migrants from neighbouring Bangladesh have fraudulently entered India’s electoral rolls.

On Friday, Defence Minister Rajnath Singh dismissed the allegations, saying the sole agenda of the opposition parties was “to destroy democratic institutions and create unrest in the country”.

“Their fight is not for electoral reform… not for Gyanesh Kumar, not for the bright future of the country’s youth,” he said at a news conference.

“Rather, this is their conspiracy to seize power by creating anarchy in the country.”

item.title: Naseem Shah’s long road to fulfilling his promise as Pakistan’s pace spearhead
item.description:
In the soft autumn light of Rawalpindi, where the stands once erupted for a boy barely old enough to drive, Naseem Shah returned to the ground that first announced him to the world.

Seven months had passed since injury forced him off the field. When he returned in the opening Twenty20 International against Sri Lanka last week, the ball still left his hand with its familiar menace.

Three wickets for 36 runs in four overs. A first-ball breakthrough. Pace touching the mid-140s. The crowd remembered. So did Pakistan.

Now three months short of his 24th birthday, Naseem has taken 155 wickets in 93 international matches. His tally includes 60 in Tests at an average of 35.13 and 60 in ODIs at 25.91, with a strike rate of 28.3. The figures speak of promise fulfilled in flashes, and of potential still waiting to fully blossom.

“I feel I’m yet to play my peak cricket,” he told PCB Digital this week. “Whatever cricket I’ve played so far, especially Test cricket, I think I lacked a few things.”

The admission carries the weight of a career lived at high velocity. Born in Mayar, Lower Dir, in February 2003, Naseem was thrust into international cricket at 16. His Test debut against Australia in Brisbane in November 2019 came before many of his peers had finished school.

Three months later, on the Rawalpindi pitch that would become part of his legend, he claimed a hat-trick against Bangladesh. At 16 years and 359 days, he became the youngest bowler to achieve the feat in Test cricket.

The country took to the slight teenager who charged in with raw aggression and an action that drew comparisons with the great fast bowlers of the past.

His early years were a whirlwind. He claimed a five-wicket haul against Sri Lanka at 16, followed by consecutive five-fors in ODIs — 5-33 against the Netherlands in August 2022 and 5-57 against New Zealand the following January. He became only the sixth Pakistan bowler to achieve the feat of taking five wickets in consecutive ODI innings.

In white-ball cricket, Naseem appeared a natural — sharp with the new ball, capable of making the old one reverse and increasingly adept at reading a batter’s intentions. Fast bowling, he now reflects, is “all about aggression and smartness”. The two, he believes, must go hand in hand.

Yet the body that produced such pace has repeatedly let him down. A back injury early in his career cost him more than a year, and shoulder problems followed.

The most painful setback came during the 2023 Asia Cup match against India, when he suffered a tendon injury that required surgery. He watched the World Cup from the sidelines as Pakistan’s campaign unfolded without one of its most threatening bowlers.

“You go back to zero whenever you are injured,” he said. “Sometimes it doesn’t even allow you to go for a run, let alone going through the motions of the game. The rehabilitation programme then becomes important. It is also critical how well you understand your body during those times.”

The latest setback came during the Pakistan Super League earlier this year. A back injury, suffered just as he was rediscovering his rhythm, ruled him out of the tournament and kept him away from the national side for seven months.

During that period of rehabilitation, involving early mornings, carefully planned strengthening exercises and mental adjustment, his understanding of fast bowling began to evolve. The teenage firebrand has become a young man who speaks of awareness, match situations and variations beyond raw speed.

“When you are young you know how to bowl fast,” he explained. “But the important thing is to have sense of what you are trying to do. There are many fast bowlers in the world who bowl 140-plus, but they are not consistent. One or two matches and injuries come.”

He has learnt that bowling at 150 kilometres per hour counts for little if runs flow freely and the body breaks down after a handful of matches. Consistency, execution at 70 or 80 per cent of maximum effort and the ability to surprise a batter with a slower ball after a verbal exchange are among the lessons injury has taught him.

In modern white-ball cricket, where pitches often favour batters and the demands of the game require constant innovation, he believes bowlers must continue to evolve.

His return against Sri Lanka offered an encouraging indication of what lies ahead. In the first T20I, he unsettled the top order before finishing the innings with precision.

In the second, although he went wicketless, he conceded only nine runs in his powerplay overs. It was the kind of disciplined spell that can make a difference in a series. Pakistan won the T20I series 2-1, with Naseem playing his part.

His attention is now turning towards the 2027 World Cup in South Africa, where Pakistan are scheduled to begin their campaign against Afghanistan on Oct 8. It would be his first senior World Cup appearance, following the disappointment of missing the 2023 tournament.

He is also part of the squad for the forthcoming ODI tri-series against England and Sri Lanka, another step in his preparations.

In 34 ODIs, he has demonstrated his ability to compete at the highest level. The challenge now is to sustain that performance over time.

“You make a goal,” he said, “and those goals keep changing with injuries and the ups and downs of a career. But I had set a goal that I want to play cricket up to a certain level. I feel my peak cricket is still ahead of me.”

Looking back, he wonders what more he might have achieved with a better understanding of pitches, his own body and the demands of the game. Looking ahead, he sees only the work that remains.

There is something compelling about the journey of the young man from the mountains of Dir. He arrived as a prodigy and has since endured the isolation of rehabilitation that fast bowlers often face.

The setbacks have been real, the absences painful and the scrutiny relentless. Yet the pace remains, the ball still moves, and his understanding of the game has deepened.

The emphasis has shifted from raw speed to longevity and impact. Pakistan need more than occasional explosive spells. They need a bowler who can deliver consistently, series after series, and take responsibility when the stakes are highest.

The 2027 World Cup is no longer a distant prospect. It is a target around which Naseem can build the next phase of his career.

For a country that has watched him rise, fall and return, the hope is that the boy who took a Test hat-trick at 16 will, as a 24-year-old, deliver the sustained excellence his talent has long promised.

The journey continues. Naseem believes his peak is still to come.

item.title: What options does Indian law provide for CEC’s removal?
item.description:
AMID growing calls for the resignation of India’s top election official Gyanesh Kumar for alleged voter roll manipulation, a key issue has come to the fore: the process of the chief election commissioner’s appointment, resignation and termination. The campaign to remove Gyanesh Kumar from office began after a newspaper report alleged that he was responsible for removing the names of 130 million voters from India’s electoral rolls — a figure slightly higher than Bangladesh’s entire voting population.

While the Congress Party, India’s “cockroach” youth movement and others demand Kumar’s resignation, which is simple enough, Kumar’s removal from office is a lengthy and complicated affair, similar to the removal of a Supreme Court judge.

Article 324 of the Indian constitution, whi­ch deals with the Election Commission, outlines the procedures for removal of the election chief. Article 324 (5) stipulates that the top election official shall not be removed fr­­om office “except in like manner and on the like grounds as a Judge of the Supreme Court”.

In India, the CEC is appointed under the Chief Election Commissioner and other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023. The CEC is appointed by the president.

The law stipulates that people who are serving or have served in positions equivalent to a secretary to the Indian government will be eligible. They also have to be “persons of integrity, who have knowledge of and experience in management and conduct of elections”. A search committee, led by the law minister, compiles a panel of five persons for consideration of the selection committee.

The election chief and commissioners are subsequently appointed by the president upon the recommendation of this selection committee, which currently consists of the prime minister, who serves as the chair, along with the leader of opposition in Lok Sabha and a minister as nominated by the prime minister.

The law governing their appointment, however, witnessed a significant change in 2023 where the constitution of the selection committee was changed. Earlier, the selection panel consisted of the prime minister, opposition leader and chief justice of India. The top judge was replaced by a union cabinet minister, for which Narendra Modi chose his home minister, Amit Shah.

Critics argue that this change increases executive influence over the appointment process, as two of the three members of the selection committee would be from the ruling party. As for resigning from office, it is a simple procedure where the election chief or any of the commissioners “may, at any time, by writing under his hand addressed to the president, resign his office”.

Removal

The election chief’s removal follows a quasi-judicial procedure in line with the procedure stipulated by the Judges Inquiry Act, 1968. Supreme Court and High Court judges can be removed on two grounds — proven misbehaviour and incapacity. A written notice must be signed by at least 100 members of the Lok Sabha or 50 members of the Rajya Sabha. The Lok Sabha Speaker or Rajya Sabha Chair examines the notice and available information, and decides to admit or refuse the motion.

If admitted, a committee is convened with one Supreme Court judge, one High Court judge and one distinguished legal expert. The election chief will have the right to defend against the allegation as the committee investigates. If the committee concludes that the charges are not proved, the motion is dropped, and the process ends.

If the committee finds that allegations are true, the report is submitted to the parliament. The motion to remove the election chief will have to carry a special majority (two-thirds of voters present and voting) in both houses, in order to pass. If the motion passes both houses, a formal address is presented to the president, who issues the official order of removal.

The election chief, Gyanesh Kumar has denied accusations of manipulating the voter list during an exercise to verify India’s one billion voters.

Bangladesh failed to vaccinate children, independent review finds
item.description:
A joint independent review team has identified gaps in childhood immunisation, depleted stocks of measles-rubella vaccines in 2025 and delays in a special vaccination campaign as reasons for the measles outbreak in Bangladesh.

The team of international and local experts also said the incumbent government’s response to the outbreak was inadequate. It found that Bangladesh had failed to vaccinate children.

The experts warned that outbreaks of other diseases, including whooping cough and diphtheria, could occur unless urgent action was taken. They recommended addressing shortcomings in local vaccination planning, filling vacant positions in the workforce and ensuring an uninterrupted supply of vaccines.

The findings were presented at a hotel in the capital on Wednesday. A Joint Independent Review Team comprising representatives of the World Health Organization (WHO), UNICEF, Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, officials from the Ministry of Health and the Expanded Programme on Immunization (EPI), and public health experts investigated and assessed various aspects of the measles outbreak, the vaccination situation and EPI activities.

The team said it would be difficult for Bangladesh to maintain its achievements and reputation in vaccination. The measles outbreak was a clear warning, it added.

The review involved international and local experts organised into nine subteams, including one national team and eight divisional teams. Each divisional team collected information from two upazilas in two districts.

The teams gathered data by visiting vaccination centres, interviewing mothers who had left vaccination centres without vaccinating their children, speaking to 10 new mothers in each area, visiting schools and madrasahs, and interviewing mothers and daughters in five households.

The 70-member team began its work on 3 October.

Wednesday’s event was primarily a workshop. Katrina Kretsinger, head of the Joint Independent Review Team, presented the main findings of the investigation and assessment. The public health expert has worked for more than 20 years with the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the WHO. Representatives of the eight divisional teams also delivered separate presentations.

At the event, Health Minister Sardar Md Sakhawat Hossain said it was necessary to verify the quality of the vaccines administered to children.

He said the entire cold chain needed to be examined, from where vaccines were manufactured and which warehouses received them to the flights and airports through which they were transported, how they were moved from ports to district level, and how they reached vaccination centres.

Addressing the international representatives present, he said, “We assume that the vaccines are of good quality. That is an assumption. But I urge you to verify their quality as well.”

Causes of the measles outbreak

In the main presentation, Katrina Kretsinger outlined the history of Bangladesh’s EPI programme and described the vaccines administered to prevent various diseases. Explaining the causes of the measles outbreak, she said most of those infected had not been vaccinated.

The independent review found that children had been left unvaccinated both during the Awami League government’s tenure and under the previous interim government.

Kretsinger said an immunity gap had developed among children before the outbreak. Under routine immunisation programmes, around 20 per cent of children are left unvaccinated each year, with some variation.

Between 2000 and 2025, a total of 849,619 children missed measles vaccination. Stocks of measles-rubella vaccines ran out in 2025.

Her presentation showed that the most recent measles-rubella vaccination campaign had been conducted in 2020. The next campaign was due in 2024 but was postponed. A decision was taken to hold it in 2025, but it did not take place that year. A typhoid vaccination campaign was conducted in 2025, while the measles-rubella campaign was eventually held in April 2026. The delay in the measles-rubella campaign was one of the reasons behind the outbreak, she said.

Kretsinger identified several other contributing factors, including Bangladesh’s high population density and social gatherings. Vaccination is administered to children aged nine months and older, but children younger than nine months are also contracting measles.

The independent review team also assessed the current government’s response to the outbreak. It concluded that the response had been inadequate and delayed. The government had not extended vaccination to everyone at risk, including children older than five years.

The presentation also appeared to indirectly question the government’s figures for patients presenting with measles symptoms and those confirmed to have the disease.

As of 12 October, samples from 93,852 people who sought treatment with measles symptoms had been tested. Measles was detected in 68,867 of them, meaning 73 per cent of those tested were positive.

The government’s figures show a much lower proportion. According to a Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) press release on Wednesday, 208,570 suspected measles patients had been admitted to hospitals across the country so far, of whom 22,840 were confirmed to have the disease. Confirmed cases accounted for 11 per cent of suspected cases.

Where the weaknesses lie

The independent review team said the measles outbreak was a warning that the population’s immunity was weakening. It described the outbreak as a test for the country and warned that, without urgent action, outbreaks of whooping cough and diphtheria would be only a matter of time. Polio could also re-emerge, it said.

The team’s presentation identified local vaccination planning as a major weakness in Bangladesh. It said the shortcomings meant that 15 to 20 per cent of children were systematically being left out of immunisation.
Vaccination workers have to administer vaccines while also maintaining records and providing counselling.

Nutrition has not received sufficient attention in vaccination programmes, the presentation said. There is also limited preparedness to deal with problems or adverse events during vaccination.

The review team said the EPI faced a significant shortage of personnel. Around 53 per cent of technician posts responsible for maintaining the cold chain were vacant, as were 34 per cent of field-level health assistant and health inspector posts. In addition, 45 per cent of positions at the EPI’s central office were vacant.

In urban areas, 90 per cent of vaccination workers were employed by non-governmental organisations, and oversight of their work was very weak, the team said.

Vaccination activities were also disrupted for seven months in 2025 because of work stoppages by vaccination workers.

What needs to be done

Local vaccination plans must be redesigned, extending down to the ward level. Vacant positions at different levels need to be filled quickly. The age limit for vaccination should be expanded, and an uninterrupted vaccine supply must be ensured. The team also recommended promptly finalising a plan for vaccine procurement after Gavi’s support ends.

Other recommendations included better coordination among organisations supporting vaccination and greater attention to urban areas. The team also proposed introducing a system to check whether children have received all required vaccines before they enrol in school.

Addressing civil surgeons from different districts who attended the event, Prime Minister’s Special Assistant SM Zia Uddin Haider said they were well aware of the problems. If civil surgeons ensured that vaccination activities were properly conducted in their respective districts, many of the problems could be resolved, he said.

Representatives of several international organisations expressed concern over the current measles situation in Bangladesh.

Gavi representative Dierk Geyl said many people in urban areas remained outside the vaccination system, often without being noticed. Vaccination efforts in cities needed to be strengthened, he added.

UNICEF’s acting representative in Dhaka, Gillian Mellsop, said the measles outbreak in 2026 was unfortunate despite Bangladesh’s strong history of vaccination. She recommended introducing a digital system to track who was receiving vaccines.

WHO Representative to Bangladesh Rajesh Narwal said Bangladesh’s vaccination system had been recognised as strong for decades. Its foundation remained solid, but modernising the system was essential.

item.title: School roof collapse kills teacher, 27 children in Pakistan
item.description:
PAKISTAN-ACCIDENT-SCHOOL

Twenty-seven pupils and a teacher were killed on Thursday after a roof collapsed at a school in the northwest Pakistani city of Peshawar, a hospital official said.

Asim Khan from Peshawar''s Lady Reading Hospital confirmed the toll to AFP, adding that over 30 people were injured, with six believed to be in a critical condition.

A spokesman for the emergency rescue service in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province said the schoolchildren were crushed and trapped after the roof gave way.

"When the Rescue 1122 emergency response teams arrived at the scene, they found that one roof had collapsed on to another, causing the classroom below to be crushed and trapping children inside," spokesman Bilal Ahmad Faizi said.

"There are concerns that more children may still be trapped beneath the rubble," he said, adding that 16 ambulances, two disaster response vehicles and more than 60 personnel were deployed to the site.

Images released by the emergency services showed rescue workers in high-vis vests scrambling to move debris, rubble and dirt.

AFP journalists saw dozens of people at the scene.

Resident Sher Ahmed said he blamed "substandard construction materials" for the tragedy, and called for a probe.

"With profound grief and sorrow, I urge the authorities to conduct a thorough investigation and take strict action against anyone found responsible so that such tragedies can be prevented in the future," he said.

''Deep sorrow''

Pakistan''s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif in a statement expressed "deep sorrow and grief over the loss of precious lives".

"The Prime Minister extends his condolences to the bereaved families and prays for them to have the strength and patience to bear this irreparable loss," the statement said.

President Asif Ali Zardari branded the roof collapse a "heartbreaking tragedy".

"In this hour of grief, the entire nation shares the sorrow of the affected families," he said in a statement.

Roof and building collapses are common across Pakistan, mainly because of poor safety standards and shoddy construction materials in the South Asian nation of more than 240 million people.

In June this year more than a dozen children were killed in a roof collapse at a tutoring centre in the eastern city of Lahore.

In 2025, 27 people were killed and 10 injured when a five-storey building collapsed in the impoverished area of Lyari in the southern city of Karachi.

item.title: Solar projects could save Tk754 crore over 20 years, assessment finds
item.description:
Bangladesh could save an estimated Tk753.75 crore over 20 years by installing solar power systems at public universities, National University-affiliated colleges and selected urban areas, according to an assessment presented in Dhaka on Thursday.
The proposed installations would have a combined capacity of 132.61 megawatt-peak (MWp) and require an estimated initial investment of Tk731 crore. They would cover 31 public universities, 150 colleges affiliated with the National University, Shailkupa municipality and Rajshahi city.
The assessment was presented at a citizen dialogue organized by the Consumers Association of Bangladesh (CAB) at the Dhaka Reporters Unity auditorium on October 15.
The proposed systems are estimated to generate 192.7 million units of electricity in the first year and around 3.7 billion units over 20 years. The assessment estimates that electricity could be generated at around Tk4 per unit, depending on the project and installation type.
The assessment identifies 52.50MWp of potential solar capacity across 31 public universities, requiring an estimated investment of Tk288 crore.
For 150 National University-affiliated colleges, it identifies a further 51.12MWp of capacity, with projected annual generation exceeding 71.4 million units of electricity.
The estimated levelized cost of electricity is Tk4.04 per unit for the university projects and Tk4.15 per unit for the college projects.
The assessment also examines installations in Shailkupa municipality and Rajshahi city. Shailkupa has an estimated potential of 4.36MWp through rooftop, ground-mounted and floating solar installations, while the potential identified for Rajshahi is 24.63MWp.
The estimated cost of electricity is Tk4 per unit for Shailkupa and Tk4.04 per unit for Rajshahi. Electricity generated through floating solar installations in Shailkupa is estimated to cost Tk4.75 per unit.
Together, the proposed installations across the universities, colleges and the two urban areas would bring the estimated capacity to 132.61MWp.
The estimates are based on site assessments, electricity-generation simulations and financial calculations. Actual generation and costs could vary depending on operating conditions, maintenance, financing arrangements and grid connectivity.
The assessment estimates that the proposed projects could generate Tk2,777 crore in electricity sales over 20 years, assuming a benchmark selling price of Tk7.50 per unit.
The projected sales revenue should not be treated as net profit, as operating expenses, financing costs, taxes, insurance and equipment replacement would have to be deducted.
The estimated savings of Tk753.75 crore are based on a comparison between an assumed alternative electricity-generation cost of Tk10 per unit and a solar electricity purchase price of Tk7.50 per unit. This produces an estimated difference of Tk2.50 per unit.
The assessment's savings estimate depends on the projected generation and the assumptions used in the financial calculations. Actual savings would depend on which sources of electricity solar power replaces and which costs can be avoided.
Power Division Secretary Mirana Mahrook, the chief guest at the dialogue, said the government was expanding solar power initiatives and had considered proposals from stakeholders.
She said the government had taken initiatives, including measures to reduce import duties, and would consider further proposals to support solar power development.
On the benchmark price for merchant power, Mahrook said Tk7.50 per unit was reasonable under current conditions. She added that the price could decline as incentives and facilities improved.
The proposed projects would allow institutions and urban areas to generate electricity through solar installations, but their financial viability would depend on the cost of equipment, long-term maintenance and arrangements for purchasing the electricity produced.
CAB energy adviser M Shamsul Alam said rooftop solar electricity could cost around Tk4.50 per unit. He said solar power could reduce dependence on fuel purchases and protect consumers from volatility in international fuel markets.
Alam also emphasized the importance of energy conservation. However, he questioned whether government agencies had sufficient capacity to maintain solar installations under the capital expenditure (capex) model.
Omera LPG Chief Executive Officer Masudur Rahim identified maintenance, equipment security and payment guarantees as barriers to investment.
He raised concerns about investor security when solar installations are placed on buildings owned by others. The theft of electrical transformers and cables was another concern, while delayed payments or unpaid electricity bills could undermine investors' ability to recover their costs.
Other entrepreneurs at the dialogue also stressed the need for reliable payment arrangements, transparent contracts and clearly defined maintenance responsibilities.
These concerns highlight the importance of establishing clear agreements among investors, electricity purchasers and the institutions hosting solar installations before projects begin operating.
The assessment indicates that technical potential and projected costs alone will not determine whether the installations succeed. Financing, secure equipment, dependable payments and clearly assigned operational responsibilities will also affect long-term performance.
The proposed installations are estimated to avoid around 2.3 million tons of carbon dioxide emissions over 20 years, based on an emissions factor of 0.62 tons per megawatt-hour.
The actual reduction would depend on the sources of electricity displaced by solar generation and the composition of the electricity grid's generation mix over the projects' operating lives.
Long-term performance would also depend on maintenance, grid connections, transparent procurement processes and independent monitoring, according to the assessment's implementation considerations.
CAB Secretary General Advocate Humayun Kabir Bhuiyan chaired the dialogue, while CAB research coordinator Shuvo Kibria moderated it.

item.title: Titumir: IMF, development partners to support Bangladesh's reform priorities
item.description:
Prime Minister's Adviser on Finance and Planning Prof Dr Rashed Al Mahmud Titumir on Thursday said that the International Monetary Fund (IMF), the World Bank and other development partners will support Bangladesh's reform programs in line with the country's own priorities and strategies.
"For the first time, international development partners are clearly expressing their willingness to support reform initiatives based on Bangladesh's priorities," he said, adding that this would create scope for the country to pursue reforms in line with its own plans.
The adviser made the remarks while briefing journalists on the sidelines of the annual meetings of the IMF and the World Bank in Bangkok.
Titumir said that, besides the IMF and the World Bank, the Asian Development Bank (ADB), the Islamic Development Bank (IsDB) and relevant agencies of China and the United States were also extending cooperation in implementing reforms based on Bangladesh's priorities.
Asked whether conditions attached to IMF loans could pose an obstacle, he said the issues would proceed through the established process. The government was working to implement each step quickly and effectively, and remained optimistic about taking effective measures in this regard.
On the IMF's economic growth and inflation forecasts, the adviser said the projections should also be viewed in terms of the potential impact on the economy if the planned reforms were not implemented.
He said differences among forecasts by international organizations were normal, adding that a review of past data suggested that the IMF's growth projections were generally somewhat conservative.
Referring to the IMF's Article IV mission report, Titumir said Bangladesh's growth forecast had been put at 4.7%. However, the government remained optimistic about achieving its budgetary growth target of 6.5%.
He said the reform agenda had been incorporated into the government's election manifesto and would also be reflected in the forthcoming five-year economic strategy.
The government believed that implementing the planned reforms would strengthen the economy's capacity.capacit, he added.
On inflation, Titumir said several factors were contributing to the persistent pressure on prices, including developments in the Middle East and long-standing inflationary pressures inherited from the past.
Reducing the cost of living for ordinary people and protecting vulnerable households remained key government priorities, he added.
The adviser acknowledged weaknesses in the previous social protection system, saying beneficiary selection had often been flawed.
"Many deserving people had been excluded, while others who were not entitled to benefits had been included. Fragmented implementation had also prevented the programmes from delivering their expected results," he added.
Citing a World Bank report, he said deficiencies in effective social protection over recent years had contributed to rising poverty.
To address the situation, he said, the government was pursuing initiatives such as the Family Card and Farmers Card to improve beneficiary selection through scientific methods and ensure that assistance reached the intended recipients.
He said the government was also emphasizing the development of digital public infrastructure to make social protection programs more effective.
Development partners had responded positively to the government's target of allocating five percent of GDP to the social sector and its plan to increase health spending, he said, adding that cooperation to support these priorities had also been discussed.
Titumir said the government aimed to raise tax collection to 10% of GDP by 2030. Restoring discipline in the banking sector, protecting depositors' interests and ensuring accountability across the financial sector were also major priorities.
He said the government had taken initiatives to return deposits to customers of Sammilito Islami Bank to ensure the security of depositors' money.
Measures would also be taken to improve transparency in banks' financial statements and balance sheets and reform the necessary legal frameworks, he added.
Highlighting past financial irregularities, Titumir said common people were bearing a heavy cost due to the plundering of funds from banks and other sectors.
According to him, around $40 billion had been looted from the banking sector.
He stressed that the money belonged to the people and those involved in financial irregularities and plundering must be held accountable.
He said both those who had siphoned off money and those who had facilitated such activities must face accountability, regardless of whether they were in Bangladesh or abroad.
A coordinated effort was needed to tackle defaulted loans and financial irregularities, he said, adding that holding those who assisted financial offenders accountable would help discourage similar crimes in the future.
The IMF and World Bank Group annual meetings are being held in Bangkok, Thailand, from October 12 to Sunday. The meetings are discussing a range of issues, including the global economic outlook, financial stability, poverty reduction and inclusive growth.

item.title: Saudi coalition says missile intercepted in Medina region
item.description:
The Saudi-led military coalition fighting Yemen’s Houthis on Thursday said it had intercepted a cruise missile in the Medina region -- home to one of Islam’s holiest cities, but the Houthis denied carrying out any such attack.
“Interception and destruction of a cruise missile in the Medina region,” coalition spokesman Turki Al-Malki wrote on X, with the statement also published by state media.
The Houthis quickly responded by saying they did not target the region on Thursday, and had previously vowed to spare the holy cities of Medina and Mecca.
Saudi Arabia has in recent days come under sustained attack from the Houthis, including a strike on Riyadh’s international airport that was the kingdom’s deadliest in years, as the war with the group escalates.
Riyadh has hit back with strikes against the Iran-backed group’s stronghold in the Yemeni capital Sanaa.
Medina, the burial place of the Prophet Mohammed and home to the Prophet’s Mosque, is one of Islam’s holiest cities alongside Mecca.
The Houthis have vowed to continue targeting airports and other sites across Saudi Arabia but on Sunday said Mecca and Medina would be spared.
“The Yemeni armed forces confirm that they have not carried out any operation today targeting Saudi territory, and that the Saudi enemy’s claims of an attack on Medina are a shameless and brazen lie,” Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree wrote on X on Thursday.
On Wednesday the Houthis said they had targeted facilities belonging to Saudi oil giant Aramco, with Saudi officials reporting a strike on a building in an area housing the energy giant’s operations center.
The Saudi-led coalition has supported Yemen’s government militarily against the Houthis since 2015 in a long-running civil war that has created a humanitarian crisis.

item.title: Shama stresses climate justice, accountability ahead of COP31
item.description:
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam on Thursday highlighted the importance of climate justice and accountability, the loss and damage fund, a just transition and green growth for Bangladesh ahead of COP31.
Speaking at a meeting on Bangladesh’s priorities and preparations for the climate conference, she called for implementing the National Action Plan and ensuring the predictable, adequate and transparent disbursement of global climate finance in line with national priorities.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs hosted the meeting with climate experts and other stakeholders, with the state minister in the chair.
Prime Minister’s Special Assistant on Environment, Forest and Climate Change Md Saimum Parvez, prominent climate experts of Bangladesh, representatives of research organizations, national and international organizations, and senior foreign ministry officials attended the meeting.
Discussions focused on the COP31 action agenda, Bangladesh’s priorities and preparations for the conference.
Shama said the Conference of the Parties (COP) provides a global platform for climate diplomacy, covering adaptation, mitigation and resilience.
She also highlighted the importance of linking the circular economy with green industry and said Bangladesh’s jute, a sustainable and biodegradable natural fibre, will be showcased at COP31.
The state minister urged stakeholders to contribute from their respective positions to strengthen Bangladesh’s stance at the conference.
The participants welcomed the ministry’s initiative, while climate experts shared their perspectives on the COP31 agenda to help shape Bangladesh’s position.
Youth representatives, who are set to participate in the conference for the first time, also shared their views, expectations and proposals to strengthen the country’s preparations.
The participants also mentioned that strategies and policies should be formulated in a holistic way so that they can be implemented beyond COP31.
They also underscored the importance of highlighting flagship projects/initiatives of the government to the world.
COP31 is going to take place in Antalya, Türkiye on November 9-20, 2026.
A Bangladeshi delegation is expected to participate in high-level sessions, negotiations and discussions.
Bangladesh also plans to present its climate priorities and achievements, with a particular focus on showcasing jute products and technology, along with the fibre’s commercial potential as a sustainable alternative to plastic.

item.title: Dhaka calls for inclusive, results-driven CICA
item.description:
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir on Thursday reaffirmed Bangladesh's commitment to advance regional cooperation among the Asian countries.
While speaking at the plenary session of the 7th Summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA) in Baku, the state minister conveyed Bangladesh's full support for CICA's transformation into a full-fledged international regional organization with a clear legal status, a strengthened Secretariat, predictable financing and effective decision-making.
In his statement, he put forward three concrete proposals on the implementation of results-oriented sectoral projects backed by formal follow-up mechanisms to build meaningful partnerships among member states, organizing more in-person events to foster wider stakeholder participation, strengthening exchanges among member states' ICT institutions and developing confidence-building measures for a safe, open and trusted digital space to address emerging challenges in ICT and AI.
This year, the 7th CICA summit is taking place under the chairmanship of Azerbaijan with the theme "A Stronger CICA: Connectivity, Digitalization, and Sustainable Growth in Asia," reflects priorities of vital importance to the peoples of Asia.
During the summit, Lao PDR became the 29th member of this Pan-Asian forum established in 1999 with a view to promoting peace, security and stability across ASIA.
The summit also endorsed the Chairmanship of Azerbaijan for 2026-28 and the appointment of Sultan Hajiyev as the next Secretary General of CICA.
Meanwhile, Bangladesh staged a walkout during the Israeli president's address at the seventh summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA) in Baku.
The Bangladesh delegation, led by State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir, walked out of the conference hall as the Israeli president began delivering his speech at the summit, said the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
Representatives of several other countries also joined the walkout, boycotting the Israeli president's address.
The delegations left the conference hall in protest during the Israeli president's speech.
The seventh CICA summit is being held in the Azerbaijani capital, bringing together leaders and senior representatives of participating countries to discuss regional cooperation, security and confidence-building measures across Asia.

item.title: Saudi Arabia accuses Iran of encouraging Houthis in latest escalation
item.description:
A Saudi foreign ministry official on Thursday accused Iran of encouraging the Houthis in the latest escalation of their fight with the kingdom, adding that the Islamic Republic continues to arm and train the group.
“Iran continues to arm, train and support the Houthi militia in violation of UN Security Council resolutions,” Dr Rayed Krimly, deputy minister for public diplomacy at the foreign ministry, said during a virtual briefing with reporters.
“We think that the escalation by the Houthis at this latest stage of the conflict is encouraged by Iran,” he later said.
The official said the kingdom however remained in communication with Iran, even if Tehran appeared unwilling to offer concessions.
“We continue to have direct communications with Iran,” Krimly told reporters.
“Overall, it doesn’t seem yet that the Iranians are able to provide the necessary concessions for a solution.”
The official went on to accuse the Houthis of refusing to meet in Oman in recent weeks as fighting ramped up between the two sides.
“At the beginning of this escalation, we asked them to meet in Muscat, Oman and they refused,” he added.
“This was the last communication which happened a few weeks ago.”
The world’s top crude oil exporter has in recent days come under sustained attack, including a strike on Riyadh’s international airport that was the deadliest in years, as the war with the Houthis dramatically escalates.
Yemen’s civil war reignited in July after a UN-brokered truce collapsed, months into a wider Middle East war that has rocked the region and roiled energy supplies and markets.
The conflict in the country has caused what the United Nations calls one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises, leaving most of the nation’s population dependent on aid.
The Saudi-led coalition has fought the Houthis since 2015 after they seized Yemen’s capital Sanaa and forced out the internationally recognized government from the city, until a UN-brokered ceasefire in 2022.

item.title: Durga Puja: BGB setting up 18 base camps for security at bordering puja mandaps
item.description:
Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) is setting up 18 base camps and strengthening patrols to ensure security at around 1,800 puja mandaps located within eight kilometres of the country's borders during Durga Puja.
BGB Director General Major General Mohammad Ashrafuzzaman Siddiqui disclosed the plan while talking to reporters after inspecting the security arrangements at the Ramna Kali Mandir in the capital on Thursday afternoon.
He said BGB personnel have already visited the mandaps and contacted puja committees in their respective areas to coordinate security measures.
“Risks of different kinds can arise at any time. We are collecting intelligence, receiving information from various agencies and working to ensure comprehensive security so that the celebrations can take place without disruption,” the BGB chief said.
He said the force will also ensure security at puja mandaps located within a few kilometres of its headquarters in Pilkhana and other battalion, sector and regional headquarters outside border areas, in coordination with police and other law enforcement agencies.
Ashrafuzzaman said the BGB regularly coordinates with the authorities of the Ramna Kali Mandir, Dhakeshwari National Temple and other nearby puja mandaps in the capital.
He said a 24/7 control room has been opened at BGB headquarters to maintain communication with puja mandaps.
The BGB director general added that the “Sharadiya Surokkha App”, developed under the Ministry of Home Affairs, will allow puja committee members and Ansar personnel deployed at the mandaps to contact law enforcement agencies in case of any problem or emergency.
The BGB will take prompt measures as necessary to maintain security and ensure peaceful and festive celebrations, he said.
Ashrafuzzaman also said intelligence gathering, risk assessment and security measures have been strengthened in coordination with intelligence agencies.
During the visit, he exchanged views with the president and other members of the Ramna Kali Mandir Sarbojonin Puja Udjapan Committee and conveyed his greetings to members of the Hindu community on the occasion of Durga Puja.
Other senior BGB officials were present during the inspection.

item.title: ‘No Kings’ October 17 protest: 2,500 rallies, marches, and parties in all 50 states urge Americans to vote early in midterm election
item.description:
The “No Kings” movement, which began as a populist protest against the Trump administration, has now morphed into a get-out-the-vote movement ahead of the U.S. midterm elections on November 3.

On Saturday, October 17, “No Kings: Vote Early” is scheduled to take place, and more than 2,500 events are on the map in all 50 states. Organizers are preparing a range of events, from protests to neighborhood block parties and cookouts, with a focus on ensuring free and fair elections in November.

Marches, rallies, and voter fairs related to early voting are scheduled for several major U.S. cities, including San Francisco, Atlanta, Washington, D.C., New York, and Los Angeles. There will also be events in Boston, Philadelphia, and Austin. (See a full list of events here.)

The day is being organized by a broad coalition of nonprofits, educators, unions, and progressive political groups. These include the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), American Federation of Teachers, Black Voters Matter Fund, 50501, Indivisible, League of Women Voters, MoveOn, Public Citizen, State Voices, and Voto Latino. (A full list of partners is available here.)

“Early and record turnout is our best chance to ensure every vote is counted and election results are too big to rig,” Joel Payne, chief communications officer for MoveOn Civic Action, tells Fast Company.

Since the beginning of President Donald Trump’s second term, No Kings protests have drawn millions of people in large cities and small towns across America. The last protest, on March 28, was attended by an estimated 9 million people.

Now organizers are taking that message to the ballot box. Unlike previous protests, the coming event will include walks to polling stations, voter planning drives, and local election defense workshops.

“In order to protect our voting rights, the ACLU has identified dozens of scenarios for election interference and voter disenfranchisement across the country and prepared to respond immediately with legal action and community mobilization,” Deirdre Schifeling, the organization’s chief political and advocacy officer, tells Fast Company. “Together with our affiliates and partners, we have built a powerful network of organizers, community leaders, and tens of thousands of volunteers who are ready to navigate attacks on our elections and assist voters.”

“No one gets to scare us out of our vote, and on October 17th, we’re showing up, fiercely and fearlessly, to show the power of the American vote,” adds Beatriz Lopez, executive director of Voto Latino.

item.title: Florida can now enforce a ban on social media accounts for kids
item.description:
The state of Florida won a key court decision Wednesday that allows it to enforce a ban on social media accounts for kids under 14 and other restrictions.

The law was one of the most restrictive in the U.S. on social media use by children when Gov. Ron DeSantis signed it in 2024.

The law implicates the First Amendment, an appeals court said, but “likely does so in a content-neutral manner.”

It would likely survive a full legal challenge “because it doesn’t burden substantially more speech than necessary to advance the important interest in protecting minors from social media addiction,” a panel from the 11th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals said in a 3-0 opinion.

The law bans social media accounts for Florida children under 14 and requires parental consent for use by kids who are 14 or 15.

Industry trade groups the Computer & Communications Industry Association and NetChoice sued Florida, arguing that the law violated the free-speech rights of social media providers and users. A judge in 2025 said the law likely was unconstitutional and granted an injunction.

That injunction was put on hold while the appeals court heard the case. The lawsuit, with the injunction now overturned, will return to federal court in Tallahassee.

The appeals court noted that the law covers social media platforms “that have been determined to induce heavy use by children, and applies only to platforms that use both algorithms and one of several addictive features.”

An email seeking comment from the Florida attorney general’s office was not immediately answered. NetChoice said it was disappointed with the decision.

“We are currently evaluating all of our options as we continue the fight to ensure Floridians’ rights to free expression online are protected, and parents remain in the driver’s seat when it comes to making decisions for their families,” said Paul Taske, a lawyer at NetChoice.

—Ed White, Associated Press
